title: The true samana
hookLine: what makes a real renunciant, and the jhana similes

lines: A LABEL ARRIVES IN A MOMENT.
cards: Engineer. Monk. A label arrives in a moment: a badge, a uniform, a line on a form.
Living up to it takes years. In a market town called Assapura, the Buddha told his monks: people call you samanas, renunciants, and when they're asked, you call yourselves that too.
So train, he says, so that the name is true, and so that what people give you bears fruit.

teach.b: This is the greater discourse at Assapura, the thirty-ninth of the Middle-Length Sayings. A samana in the Buddha's India was anyone who had left home to seek freedom, a wandering renunciant.
The Buddha lists what makes the name real, one step at a time: a sense of shame and fear of doing wrong. Clean conduct in body, speech and mind. An honest way of living.
Guarding the senses. Eating in moderation. Staying awake to practice.
Mindfulness in everything, even walking and dressing.

teach.h: STEP BY STEP, AND DON'T STOP HERE
teach.b: After each step he warns them: don't stop here, thinking we've done enough. Then the hindrances fall away, and he describes the deep stillness of meditation, the jhanas, with four pictures.
The first is like a bath attendant kneading soap powder with water in a bowl, until the whole ball is moist, inside and out, and nothing leaks.
The second, a lake fed by a spring from below, cool water welling up through the whole lake. The third, lotuses that grow underwater, soaked in cool water from root to tip.

teach.h: SOAP, A SPRING, LOTUSES, A WHITE CLOTH
teach.b: The fourth, a person sitting wrapped head to foot in a clean white cloth. Each picture is fuller and quieter than the one before.

teach.h: ONLY THE FREED MIND EARNS THE NAME
teach.b: Only when the mind is fully freed, the Buddha says, can someone truly be called a samana.
The weight isn't on the robe, the shaved head, or what people call you. It's on what's actually happening inside, through and through, like water in a ball of soap.

how: Meditation teachers use MN 39's four jhana similes (the soap ball, the spring-fed lake, the underwater lotuses, the white cloth) to describe deepening states of stillness, and monastics recall that the robe alone doesn't make the renunciant.

o: a village elder who settles disputes
a temple priest who performs rituals
a renunciant who left home to seek freedom

p: soap powder kneaded until fully moist
a lake fed by a spring from below

s: the robe and shaved head make someone a samana
the Buddha puts the weight on the trained and freed mind, not on what people call you.
after each step the Buddha warns: don't stop here
he tells them not to think they've done enough, all the way to freedom.
a samana was a temple priest in the Buddha's India
a samana was a wandering renunciant who had left home to seek freedom.

games.q: you've kept the precepts, guarded your senses and eaten in moderation. people praise you as a true samana. what does the Buddha tell monks in your place?
o: don't stop here: there's more to do.
leave the order; you don't need it now.
games.why: at every stage, the Buddha warns against thinking 'we've done enough'. only the fully freed mind makes the name samana true.

practice: Choose one label you wear, friend, parent, professional, kind person, spiritual person, and let one concrete act come to mind that makes it true on an ordinary day, not a good one.
Then set the label down, rest in the breath, and let ease spread through the body slowly, the way water spreads through soap powder.

wordCard.voice: samana. A renunciant made real, not by the name or the robe, but by a mind steadily trained and finally freed.

orig.note: Pali samana (Sanskrit sramana): a renunciant, one who has left home to seek freedom.

carryVoice: Your line: not the label. The robe is given; the freedom is trained. That's day four hundred thirty-five.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 39, Maha-Assapura Sutta (the greater discourse at Assapura)
